title: Herod's laughter (Luke 23:1–12)
hookLine: sent to Herod, he says nothing, and two enemies become friends that day

lines: I FIND NO FAULT IN THIS MAN.
cards: Morning. The council brings Jesus to Pilate, the Roman governor, with charges that would worry any Roman: he stirs up the nation, forbids paying taxes to Caesar, calls himself a king.
Luke's readers have already heard him on taxes: render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Pilate asks one question and announces: "I find no fault in this man." They keep pressing.
He started in Galilee, they say. Pilate hears a way out. Galilee belongs to Herod, and Herod happens to be in Jerusalem.

teach.b: This is Herod the tetrarch, ruler of Galilee. Earlier in Luke he's the man who says he beheaded John the Baptist, and Jesus once called him that fox. Herod is thrilled.
He'd wanted to see Jesus for a long time, and hoped to see him do a miracle.

He fires questions, many words, the King James says. And then: "he answered him nothing." Jesus has talked his whole way through this Gospel, to crowds, to sinners, to Pharisees at dinner, and soon to a thief on a cross.
Before this man he goes silent. Some readers hear an echo of Isaiah's servant, brought as a lamb to the slaughter, who opened not his mouth. The chief priests and scribes stand by, accusing him hard.
So Herod and his soldiers turn to mockery. They treat him with contempt, laugh at him, dress him in a gorgeous robe like a costume king, and send him back to Pilate.
Then a bitter line found in no other Gospel: "And the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together: for before they were at enmity between themselves."
Two rulers who couldn't stand each other find common ground in a joke at a silent man's expense.
Luke doesn't explain the silence. Some readers hear dignity: some questions don't deserve an answer. Others hear refusal: he will not perform for a ruler who only wants a show.
Either way, the miracle Herod hoped for never comes.

how: Churches that follow a three-year cycle of readings hear Luke's account of the trial, Herod's scene included, on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke; some readers connect Jesus's silence with the servant of Isaiah 53.

Herod's territory, so send him there

s: the accusers said Jesus forbade paying taxes to Caesar
though in Luke he had said render unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's.
Jesus gave Herod a long answer
Herod questioned him in many words, and he answered him nothing.
Pilate and Herod had been friends for years
Luke says they had been enemies, and became friends that same day.

games.q: you stand before a ruler who has wanted to see you for a long time. he's hoping for a miracle and asking question after question. what do you do?
o: do a sign, and maybe go free.
games.why: "he answered him nothing." Herod and his soldiers mock him, dress him in a gorgeous robe, and send him back to Pilate.

practice: Think of a place where you get baited, a comment section, a relative who likes to poke, a coworker's jokes, and picture the moment the jab lands: the heat rising, the reply forming.
Now let the moment pass, not sulking, not plotting, simply not performing, and breathe through it. If you pray, you can ask God for that kind of quiet.

wordCard.voice: Herod's laughter. The ruler who wanted a miracle got silence, and answered it with mockery and a borrowed robe.

orig.note: Greek: treating as nothing, with contempt. what Herod does to Jesus in Luke 23:11.

carryVoice: Your line: he answered nothing. Silence, right where Herod wanted a show. See you tomorrow.
